claim: Maintenance of a quiescent and organotypically-differentiated layer of blood vessel-lining endothelial cells (EC) is vital for human health.
source: Maintenance of a quiescent and organotypically-differentiated layer of blood vessel-lining endothelial cells (EC) is vital for human health.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established scientific understanding about endothelial cell function.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of vascular quiescence remain largely elusive.
source: Yet, the molecular mechanisms of vascular quiescence remain largely elusive.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as understood by the authors.

claim: Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 2,216 differentially expressed genes during the acquisition of vascular quiescence.
source: Comparative transcriptome analysis identified 2,216 differentially expressed genes with pronounced regulation of genes mediating the induction of immune mechanisms, metabolism and phagosome pathways as well as the repression of genes controlling cell cycle, developmental angiogenesis, extracellular matrix interactions and cell contraction (Reactome-based analysis) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript and visualized in Figure 1C.

claim: 722 genes were induced during acquisition of EC quiescence.
source: Hierarchical clustering of differentially expressed genes and functional annotation by Reactome overlap analysis of the 722 induced and 1,494 repressed genes regulated during the acquisition of EC quiescence.
evidence: This is directly stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 1,494 genes were repressed during acquisition of EC quiescence.
source: Hierarchical clustering of differentially expressed genes and functional annotation by Reactome overlap analysis of the 722 induced and 1,494 repressed genes regulated during the acquisition of EC quiescence.
evidence: This is directly stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: JAK-STAT signaling was most significantly enriched (p=5.7×10-11) in an EC quiescence network.
source: Importantly, it resulted in further specification of immune system regulation, as JAK-STAT signaling was most significantly enriched (p=5.7×10-11) in an EC quiescence network with most factors being induced, putatively mediating the repression of the pro-angiogenic growth factors Fgf7 and Fgf10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by interactome analysis and statistical enrichment testing.

claim: EdU incorporation assays verified the almost complete arrest of cell proliferation in adult EC.
source: EdU incorporation assays verified the almost complete arrest of cell proliferation in adult EC (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sixteen pro-angiogenic molecules were down-regulated during acquisition of vascular quiescence.
source: Sixteen pro-angiogenic molecules were down-regulated and eight anti-angiogenic molecules were up-regulated during acquisition of vascular quiescence (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Eight anti-angiogenic molecules were up-regulated during acquisition of vascular quiescence.
source: Sixteen pro-angiogenic molecules were down-regulated and eight anti-angiogenic molecules were up-regulated during acquisition of vascular quiescence (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The TGFβ pathway was identified as the most concordantly downregulated signaling pathway during acquisition of vascular quiescence.
source: Among these angiogenesis-regulating molecules, the TGFβ pathway was identified as the most concordantly downregulated signaling pathway with repression of matrix-associated latent TGFβ-binding proteins (Ltbp2, Ltbp3, Ltbp4) and receptors (Tgfbr2, Bmpr1) as well as upregulation of the inhibitory Smads, Smad6 and Smad7 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and pathway analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Upstream analysis revealed TGFß1 as the most significantly inhibited growth factor during acquisition of vascular quiescence.
source: Correspondingly, upstream analysis of the complete set of differentially expressed genes including activation state prediction of the corresponding upstream regulator revealed TGFß1 as the most significantly inhibited growth factor (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: About 10% of chromatin modifying enzymes were differentially expressed with the majority being repressed in adult EC.
source: About 10% of CMEs were differentially expressed with the majority being repressed in adult EC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), including the de novo DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a and four additional DNA methylation modifiers (Gadd45a, Tet1, Fos, Uhrf1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis of chromatin modifying enzymes.

claim: There was a significant increase of CpGs with >80% methylation level in adult EC compared to infant EC (p=6.87×10−6).
source: Bioinformatic analysis revealed a significant increase of CpGs with >80% methylation level in adult EC compared to infant EC (p=6.87×10−6) demonstrating a global increase in CpG methylation during the transition to vascular quiescence (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on T-WGBS data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: DNA methylation changes resulted in more than 1.4M differentially methylated CpGs (DMCs).
source: In total, DNA methylation changes resulted in more than 1.4M differentially methylated CpGs (DMCs).
evidence: This is based on T-WGBS data analysis.

claim: 68,184 consecutive DMCs with a 10% methylation difference were identified.
source: Retaining only the consecutive DMCs (68,184) with a 10% methylation difference showed a significant intragenic enrichment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on filtering and analysis of T-WGBS data.

claim: 68,184 consecutive DMCs gave rise to 18,333 differentially methylated regions (DMRs).
source: These DMCs gave rise to 18,333 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on DMR calling from T-WGBS data.

claim: Young adults acquired a gain of methylation in 54% of DMRs and a loss of methylation in 46% of DMRs during acquisition of quiescence (applying 10% threshold).
source: Applying a threshold of 10% methylation difference, young adults acquired a gain of methylation in 54% of DMRs and a loss of methylation in 46% of DMRs during acquisition of quiescence (20% gain and 80% loss, respectively, when applying 30% as threshold) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMR data from T-WGBS.

claim: Both loss and gain of methylation DMRs were depleted on transcription start sites (TSS), but enriched up- and downstream (10–100 kb distant) from the TSS.
source: Both, loss and gain of methylation DMRs were depleted on transcription start sites (TSS), but enriched up- and downstream (10–100 kb distant) from the TSS (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on genomic location analysis of DMRs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was an overall significant enrichment of DMRs in introns (OR 2.65, p<0.0001), most prominent in intron 1–3 of a given gene.
source: There was an overall significant enrichment of DMRs in introns (OR 2.65, p<0.0001), most prominent in intron 1–3 of a given gene (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on statistical enrichment analysis of DMR genomic locations.

claim: Hypomethylated DMRs were overrepresented in introns and underrepresented in intergenic regions.
source: Notably, hypomethylated DMRs were overrepresented in introns and underrepresented in intergenic regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of DMR distribution shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: DMRs coincide with putative enhancer regions (H3K4me1 positive regions, enhancer-promoter units [EPU], DNase hypersensitive regions) but not with transcription start sites.
source: Overlap of the DMRs with lung-identified genomic regulatory features (Shen et al., 2012; Yue et al., 2014) further specified the DMRs to coincide with putative enhancer regions (H3K4me1 positive regions, enhancer-promoter units [EPU], DNase hypersensitive regions) but not with transcription start sites (CpG islands, TSS defined by FANTOM consortium, H3K4me3 positive regions) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis with published genomic regulatory features and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Functional annotation of genes next to hypomethylated DMRs revealed signaling pathways controlling vascular patterning (semaphorin interactions) and development/homeostasis (TGFβ family signaling).
source: The functional annotation of genes next to hypomethylated DMRs revealed signaling pathways controlling vascular patterning (semaphorin interactions) and development/homeostasis (TGFβ family signaling) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis using the GREAT tool on DMR data.

claim: 94% of the hypomethylated DMRs affecting genes of semaphorin and TGFβ family signaling pathways were located in intragenic regions with eight DMRs per gene on average.
source: Notably, 94% of the hypomethylated DMRs affecting genes of these pathways were located in intragenic regions with eight DMRs per gene on average (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A , left) resulting in DMR clustering (more than five DMRs per gene locus) in more than 36% of the affected genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMR distribution within genes of specific pathways.

claim: More than 36% of genes affected by hypomethylated DMRs in semaphorin and TGFβ family signaling pathways showed DMR clustering (more than five DMRs per gene locus).
source: Notably, 94% of the hypomethylated DMRs affecting genes of these pathways were located in intragenic regions with eight DMRs per gene on average (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A , left) resulting in DMR clustering (more than five DMRs per gene locus) in more than 36% of the affected genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMR distribution within genes shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 56% of the hypermethylated DMRs were located in intragenic regions with on average two DMRs per gene.
source: Contrary, 56% of the hypermethylated DMRs were located in intragenic regions with on average two DMRs per gene (only 5.3% of genes harbored five or more hypermethylated DMRs).
evidence: This is based on analysis of hypermethylated DMR distribution.

claim: Only 5.3% of genes harbored five or more hypermethylated DMRs.
source: Contrary, 56% of the hypermethylated DMRs were located in intragenic regions with on average two DMRs per gene (only 5.3% of genes harbored five or more hypermethylated DMRs).
evidence: This is based on analysis of hypermethylated DMR clustering.

claim: Genes in the vicinity of gain of methylation DMRs were annotated as endothelial fate control genes (NOTCH signaling).
source: Furthermore, genes in the vicinity of gain of methylation DMRs were annotated as endothelial fate control genes (NOTCH signaling) (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A right).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation analysis of genes near hypermethylated DMRs.

claim: 10% (446) of the affected genes contained more than five intragenic DMRs corresponding to 44% (5,180) of all intragenic DMRs.
source: The ranking of all genes according to the number of intragenic DMRs further demonstrated that (i) 10% (446) of the affected genes contained more than five intragenic DMRs corresponding to 44% (5,180) of all intragenic DMRs and (ii) 68% of the clustered DMRs showed loss of methylation (Figure 4D, bottom).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of DMR distribution across genes.

claim: 68% of the clustered DMRs showed loss of methylation.
source: The ranking of all genes according to the number of intragenic DMRs further demonstrated that (i) 10% (446) of the affected genes contained more than five intragenic DMRs corresponding to 44% (5,180) of all intragenic DMRs and (ii) 68% of the clustered DMRs showed loss of methylation (Figure 4D, bottom).
evidence: This is based on analysis of methylation direction in clustered DMRs.

claim: Enrichment analysis confirmed that DMR clusters were overrepresented in genes of TGFβ and semaphorin signaling, particularly in Smad6, Smad7 and Sema6a with up to 61 DMRs in one gene.
source: Furthermore, enrichment analysis among this ranked list of genes confirmed that DMR clusters were overrepresented in genes of TGFβ and semaphorin signaling, particularly in Smad6, Smad7 and Sema6a with up to 61 DMRs in one gene (Figures 3G 4D, top, and 4E).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis and visualization of DMR clusters in specific genes.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed an enrichment of genes with hypomethylated DMRs among the genes induced in adult EC independent of the genomic loci of one or several DMRs.
source: The correlation of quiescence-related expression and methylation profiles by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed an enrichment of genes with hypomethylated DMRs (young adult vs. infant EC) among the genes induced in adult EC independent of the genomic loci of one or several DMRs.
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis correlating methylation and expression data.

claim: Genes with hypermethylated DMRs were overrepresented among the genes upregulated in infant EC.
source: Conversely, genes with hypermethylated DMRs were overrepresented among the genes upregulated in infant EC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was an increasing overlap of transcriptome and epigenome when scoring genes on the basis of intragenic DMRs and even more so when scoring based on clustered DMRs.
source: In line with this, there was an unexpected high overlap of differentially expressed genes and genes affected by DNA methylation changes. Notably, we identified an increasing overlap of transcriptome and epigenome, when scoring genes on the basis of intragenic DMRs and even more so when scoring based on clustered DMRs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between RNA-seq and T-WGBS data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Smad6 and Smad7 contained the largest intragenic cluster of hypomethylated DMRs and showed significant induction during transition to quiescence in lung EC.
source: Among these, Smad6 and Smad7 contained the largest intragenic cluster of hypomethylated DMRs and showed significant induction during transition to quiescence in lung EC (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on combined analysis of DMR data and RNA-seq data.

claim: A strong decrease in R-SMAD (receptor-regulated SMADs, SMAD2/3 and SMAD1/5/8) phosphorylation was detected in adult lung tissue.
source: Corresponding to the observed lung endothelial upregulation of Smad6 and Smad7 during acquisition of quiescence, we detected a strong decrease in R-SMAD (receptor-regulated SMADs, SMAD2/3 and SMAD1/5/8) phosphorylation in adult lung tissue confirming an inhibition of TGFβ family signaling in adult mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The upregulation of Smad6 and Smad7 during acquisition of vascular quiescence was not restricted to the lung, but also detected in EC isolated from adult mouse brain and heart.
source: The upregulation of Smad6 and Smad7 during acquisition of vascular quiescence was not restricted to the lung, but also detected in EC isolated from adult mouse brain and heart (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on qPCR validation in multiple tissues shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: R-SMAD phosphorylation was decreased in brain and heart suggesting that TGFβ signaling may vessel bed independently act as global regulator of vascular quiescence.
source: Correspondingly, R-SMAD phosphorylation was decreased in these organs suggesting that TGFβ signaling may vessel bed independently act as global regulator of vascular quiescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot analysis in multiple tissues and represents an inference about the global role of TGFβ signaling.

claim: TGFβ family ligands were consistently higher in adult organs.
source: TGFβ family ligands were consistently higher in adult organs indicating that regulation of vascular quiescence is achieved through cell intrinsic blocking of the downstream signaling machinery, that is by downregulation of receptors and upregulation of inhibitory SMADs.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of ligand levels in different tissues.

claim: Regulation of vascular quiescence is achieved through cell intrinsic blocking of the downstream signaling machinery, that is by downregulation of receptors and upregulation of inhibitory SMADs.
source: TGFβ family ligands were consistently higher in adult organs indicating that regulation of vascular quiescence is achieved through cell intrinsic blocking of the downstream signaling machinery, that is by downregulation of receptors and upregulation of inhibitory SMADs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ligands are higher in adults while signaling is reduced.

claim: Forced expression of SMAD6 or SMAD7 in cultured EC led to the reduction of SMAD2/3 and SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation upon ligand stimulation.
source: Forced expression of SMAD6 or SMAD7 in cultured EC, but not gene silencing, led to the reduction of SMAD2/3 and SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation upon ligand stimulation (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot analysis of HUVEC with forced expression of SMAD6/7 shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Cells overexpressing both SMAD6 and SMAD7 showed reduced viability upon prolonged cell culture.
source: Cells overexpressing both, SMAD6 and SMAD7 showed reduced viability upon prolonged cell culture, which was confirmed by MTT assay (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on MTT assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Proliferation and migration of EC overexpressing SMAD6 and SMAD7 was reduced.
source: Proliferation and migration of EC overexpressing SMAD6 and SMAD7 was reduced confirming the limited angiogenic potential of SMAD6 and SMAD7 expressing cells (Figure 5F and G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on EdU incorporation assays and scratch wound assays shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Endothelial cells are long-lived cells of the mesodermal lineage that line the inside of all blood vessels forming a single layer of organotypically-differentiated cells.
source: Endothelial cells (EC) are long-lived cells of the mesodermal lineage that line the inside of all blood vessels forming a single layer of organotypically-differentiated cells (Augustin and Koh, 2017; Deanfield et al., 2007; Rafii et al., 2016; Regan and Aird, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: EC acquire a quiescent state during the transition to adulthood from which they can switch back to the activated phenotype resulting in disease-associated angiogenesis.
source: Unlike unidirectional differentiation programs of short-lived epithelial cells, EC acquire a quiescent state during the transition to adulthood from which they can switch back to the activated phenotype resulting in disease-associated angiogenesis (Hobson and Denekamp, 1984; Marcelo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of the quiescent EC phenotype is a hallmark of vascular dysfunction and a commonality of diverse life-threatening diseases ranging from sepsis, atherosclerosis to cancer.
source: Loss of this EC phenotype is a hallmark of vascular dysfunction and a commonality of diverse life-threatening diseases ranging from sepsis, atherosclerosis to cancer (Carmeliet and Jain, 2011; Gimbrone and García-Cardeña, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Major and socioeconomically important chronic diseases are characterized by a loss of the quiescent EC phenotype, like age-dependent macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy.
source: Likewise, major and socioeconomically important chronic diseases are characterized by a loss of the quiescent EC phenotype, like age-dependent macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: This is based on established medical knowledge about these diseases.

claim: Vascular targeted therapies for such conditions are mostly aimed at interfering with EC activation programs.
source: Vascular targeted therapies for such conditions are mostly aimed at interfering with EC activation programs (Krzystolik et al., 2002; Tanabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on therapeutic approaches.

claim: EC quiescence is an active process, as it not only involves the absence of activators but also microenvironmental factors as well as cell intrinsic mechanisms.
source: EC quiescence is an active process, as it not only involves the absence of activators but also microenvironmental factors as well as cell intrinsic mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement based on current understanding in the field.

claim: Matricellular factors, contact with pericytes and hemodynamic forces act as microenvironmental determinants of vascular maturation.
source: Matricellular factors, contact with pericytes and hemodynamic forces act as microenvironmental determinants of vascular maturation (Armulik et al., 2011; Baeyens et al., 2016; Davis et al., 2015; Stratman et al., 2017; Yousif et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: TGFß family signaling has been described to exert both pro- and anti-angiogenic functions and to contextually cooperate with NOTCH signaling in the regulation of angiogenesis.
source: For instance, TGFß family signaling has been described to exert both, pro-and anti-angiogenic functions and to contextually cooperate with NOTCH signaling in the regulation of angiogenesis (Cai et al., 2012; Dyer et al., 2014; Goumans et al., 2003; Goumans et al., 2002; Larrivée et al., 2012; Mallet et al., 2006; Mouillesseaux et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research showing context-dependent effects.

claim: No unbiased genome-wide systems biological effort from in vivo isolated EC has been made so far to identify the transcriptomic signatures associated with the acquisition and maintenance of EC quiescence.
source: Yet, no unbiased genome-wide systems biological effort from in vivo isolated EC has been made so far to identify the transcriptomic signatures associated with the acquisition and maintenance of EC quiescence.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: DNA methylation acts in concert with other epigenetic marks in defining chromatin states which create gene active and silenced compartments in the genome.
source: DNA methylation acts in concert with other epigenetic marks in defining chromatin states which create gene active and silenced compartments in the genome (Jones, 2012; Soshnev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Epigenetic alterations play increasingly recognized important roles in the control of cellular differentiation processes.
source: Moreover, considering the increasingly recognized important roles of epigenetic alterations in the control of cellular differentiation processes (Boland et al., 2014; Cabezas-Wallscheid et al., 2014; Lipka et al., 2014), crucial molecular mediators of vessel maturation and EC quiescence may also be regulated by epigenetic mechanisms, which in EC have similarly not been studied in an unbiased genome-wide approach.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on epigenetics in differentiation.

claim: The purity of cell sorting was controlled by the validation of marker gene expression.
source: The purity of cell sorting was controlled by the validation of marker gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological validation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The phenotypic shift in marker expression (CD31/PECAM1 and CD34) between infant and young adult EC reflected the size of the corresponding EC.
source: The phenotypic shift in marker expression (CD31/PECAM1 and CD34) between infant and young adult EC reflected the size of the corresponding EC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The average transcriptome coverage was 37.8 ± 4.
source: The average transcriptome coverage was 37.8 ± 4.
evidence: This is a technical quality metric from the RNA-seq experiment.

claim: T-WGBS data were highly reproducible in MassARRAY using independent biological replicates.
source: T-WGBS data were highly reproducible in MassARRAY using independent biological replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on validation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: SMAD6 and SMAD7 have originally been identified as vascular SMADs.
source: Interestingly, SMAD6 and SMAD7 have originally been identified as vascular SMADs (Topper et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: SMAD6 and SMAD7 induction upon laminar shear stress highlights the importance of blood flow in maintaining the quiescent vascular phenotype.
source: Their induction upon laminar shear stress highlights the importance of blood flow in maintaining the quiescent vascular phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known response of SMAD6/7 to shear stress.

claim: Smad6 has recently been described to act anti-angiogenic in sprouting assays.
source: Smad6 has recently been described to act anti-angiogenic in sprouting assays (Mouillesseaux et al., 2016) and Smad7 has been shown to inhibit peritoneal angiogenesis (Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Smad7 has been shown to inhibit peritoneal angiogenesis.
source: Smad6 has recently been described to act anti-angiogenic in sprouting assays (Mouillesseaux et al., 2016) and Smad7 has been shown to inhibit peritoneal angiogenesis (Peng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genetic deletion of Smad6 leads to major cardiovascular defects with partial prenatal mortality.
source: Correspondingly, genetic deletion of Smad6 or Smad7 leads to major cardiovascular defects with partial prenatal mortality (Smad6) (Galvin et al., 2000) or to massive growth retardation with reduced viability (Smad7) (Tojo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Genetic deletion of Smad7 leads to massive growth retardation with reduced viability.
source: Correspondingly, genetic deletion of Smad6 or Smad7 leads to major cardiovascular defects with partial prenatal mortality (Smad6) (Galvin et al., 2000) or to massive growth retardation with reduced viability (Smad7) (Tojo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Vegfa was significantly higher expressed in adult EC compared to infant EC.
source: Surprisingly, the ligand Vegfa was significantly higher expressed in adult EC compared to infant EC.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: High expression of VEGFA has also been described in the adult brain.
source: High expression of VEGFA has also been described in the adult brain (Licht and Keshet, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Autocrine VEGF has been proposed to be essential for EC survival thereby fulfilling homeostatic functions.
source: Autocrine VEGF has been proposed to be essential for EC survival thereby fulfilling homeostatic functions.
evidence: This is based on established understanding in the field.

claim: Analyses of genetically engineered mice specifically lacking EC-produced VEGF indicate that paracrine VEGF does not compensate for autocrine VEGF.
source: In fact, analyses of genetically engineered mice specifically lacking EC-produced VEGF indicate that paracrine VEGF does not compensate for autocrine VEGF (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genetic studies.

claim: Expression of the VEGF decoy receptor Flt1/Vegfr1 was significantly increased (but below threshold of 1.75x) during acquisition of quiescence.
source: Conversely, expression of the VEGF decoy receptor Flt1/Vegfr1 (Boucher et al., 2017; Fong et al., 1995; Kappas et al., 2008; Kearney et al., 2002) was in the present study significantly increased (but below threshold of 1.75x) during acquisition of quiescence.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis with citations supporting the role of Flt1 as a decoy receptor.

claim: The expression of the primary VEGF signal transducing receptor Kdr/Vegfr2 was not significantly changed during acquisition of quiescence.
source: Since the expression of the primary VEGF signal transducing receptor Kdr/Vegfr2 was neither in RNA-seq nor in qPCR validation data significantly changed, this results in an increased VEGFR1/VEGFR2 ratio in adults.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and qPCR data analysis.

claim: The increased Flt1 expression and unchanged Kdr expression results in an increased VEGFR1/VEGFR2 ratio in adults.
source: Since the expression of the primary VEGF signal transducing receptor Kdr/Vegfr2 was neither in RNA-seq nor in qPCR validation data significantly changed, this results in an increased VEGFR1/VEGFR2 ratio in adults.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative expression levels of the two receptors.

claim: VEGF signaling is not dominantly regulated during the transition to vascular quiescence but instead undergoes specific and situation-specific dynamic regulation.
source: Altogether, these data imply that VEGF signaling is not dominantly regulated during the transition to vascular quiescence but instead undergoes specific and situation-specific dynamic regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complex pattern of VEGF pathway component expression.

claim: This study has for the first time established the transcriptomic and epigenetic landscape of vascular quiescence in primary lung EC.
source: In conclusion, the present study has for the first time established the transcriptomic and epigenetic landscape of vascular quiescence in primary lung EC that might also apply to EC of other tissues.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty and scope of the study.

claim: Vascular quiescence is comprehensively regulated on both transcriptional and DNA methylation level converging on the prominent inhibition of TGFß family signaling in adult EC.
source: These findings reveal that vascular quiescence is comprehensively regulated on both transcriptional and DNA methylation level converging on the prominent inhibition of TGFß family signaling in adult EC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined transcriptomic and epigenomic data.

claim: The acquisition of the resting EC phenotype is accompanied by a dynamic balance of activating and inhibiting pathways.
source: Moreover, the acquisition of the resting EC phenotype is accompanied by a dynamic balance of activating and inhibiting pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of pathway regulation observed.

claim: The study lays a foundation for mechanistic and functional studies of individual genes and complex gene signatures involved in the transition from the activated to the quiescent phenotype and vice versa.
source: The study thereby lays a foundation for mechanistic and functional studies of individual genes and complex gene signatures involved in the transition from the activated to the quiescent phenotype and vice versa.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact and utility of the study.

claim: Proximal promoter DNA methylation regulates EC gene expression and thereby controls EC fate.
source: It has been described that proximal promoter DNA methylation regulates EC gene expression and thereby controls EC fate (Shirodkar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Flow-dependent DNA methylation changes in vessel wall cells have been shown to be enriched in GC-rich, 5' untranslated, and exonic regions.
source: Similarly, flow-dependent DNA methylation changes in vessel wall cells have been shown to be enriched in GC-rich, 5' untranslated, and exonic regions (Davies et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2015a; Jiang et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies in EC have determined an enrichment of promoter-associated changes in DNA methylation that coincide with gene regulation.
source: These previous studies in EC have determined an enrichment of promoter-associated changes in DNA methylation that coincide with gene regulation.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings.

claim: Some studies suggest intragenic DNA methylation changes play a role in alternative promoter usage or splicing.
source: Although little is known about the impact of intragenic DNA methylation changes on gene expression, some studies suggest a role in alternative promoter usage or splicing (Kulis et al., 2013; Maunakea et al., 2013; Maunakea et al., 2010; Shukla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Atherosclerosis progression in human appears to be associated with a distinct gain of methylation signature.
source: Notably, while we identified a more prominent loss than gain of methylation during acquisition of quiescence, atherosclerosis progression in human appears to be associated with a distinct gain of methylation signature (Zaina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on atherosclerosis.

claim: Epigenetic modifications play an important role in the regulation of EC functions.
source: Altogether, these data highlight the important role of epigenetic modifications in the regulation of EC functions and have led to the identification of distinct genomic regions with crucial regulatory potential that will serve as a foundation for further functional studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: The study identified distinct genomic regions with crucial regulatory potential that will serve as a foundation for further functional studies.
source: Altogether, these data highlight the important role of epigenetic modifications in the regulation of EC functions and have led to the identification of distinct genomic regions with crucial regulatory potential that will serve as a foundation for further functional studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the findings.

claim: Molecules of the VEGF pathway were both transcriptionally and epigenetically not identified as being significantly differentially regulated during the transition to EC quiescence.
source: Remarkably, molecules of the VEGF pathway, the master regulator of angiogenesis induction, were both, transcriptionally and epigenetically not identified as being significantly differentially regulated during the transition to EC quiescence.
evidence: This is based on analysis of both RNA-seq and T-WGBS data.
